# videoskillet.js — every control

Generated by scripts/docgen.mjs from the app’s own control table. The name in
brackets is what the panel and the rest of the docs call the control; the key
in front of it is what #set= and #mod= take. A value outside the range is
clamped, not refused.

Modulation sources for #mod=: sine, triangle, walk, smooth, hold, lorenz, level, hit, trig.
Up to 8 routings, rate 0.02..10 Hz, depth 0..1.

Presets for #preset=: clean, vhs, protectedTape, wornTape, pictureSearch, stuckTape, trackingBand, servoHunt, hueRidesTheLight, overDeviatedWhite, oneLineBack, broadcast, mistunedRf, fringeReception, ignitionStorm, deadChannel, dimmerHash, scrambledChannel, ssavi, verticalHoldGone, bentScan, supplyChaos, fullCollapse, bassSmack, lineNineteen, collapsedAxes, mixerLoop, strobeTrails, keyLoop, fbBloom, woundSpiral, shadowLadder, ladderClimb, subcarrierSiren, huntingServos, meltdown, zoomBloom, tunnelOut, spiral, subcarrierComb, ringLoop, ringLadder, ringStorm, ringOnTheBeat, invertedRungs, ringInTheHighlights, ringInTheShadows, warpInTheHighlights, warpInTheShadows, rungsInTheLight, ringingInTheHighlights, chasingItsOwnColour, carvedByTheLivePicture, theHoleTheSubjectKeeps, itOnlyEatsTheRed, theWrongClock, colourInTheDark, greyUnderTheColour, lightBecomesHue, theSecondCrystal, layeredByBrightness, intermodLoop, whereTheProductsLand, servoWarp, bothLoops, runaway, syncInTheLoop, lorenzLoop, strobeBloom, cleanDissolve, dirtyMix, ringMix, outOfVolts, pauseFight, pirateFeed, negativeDrifter, houseDeckHeld, differenceKey, greenScreen, matteFlood, keySweep, keyIntoTheLoop, wipeFight, negative, signalAndGroundSwapped, sVideoMiswire, noTerminator, daisyChained, looseConnector, bentEnhancer, contourLines, pouredColour, silkscreen, falseColour, blockColour, litAtTheEdges, contoursOnContours, ringPlaid, twoMultipliers, punchIn, rainbowStorm, neonTube, strobedTube, roundTube, greenTerminal, radarTube, noseAgainstTheGlass, bentDetailer, howlroundLoom, falseSync, paperclipChroma, blackRestore, magnetised, misconverged, transmissionFault, nightMonitor, everyColourButOne, pastTheYoke, arcStorm, railSlam, chromaRails, outOfHeadroom, soundAtTheRails, lightThatStays, servicePosition, splitPhase, wiggledPlugs, threeServos, hairOffTheCrystal, clampInThePicture, colourAStepRight, aimedAtTheVcr, oneHeadPacked, tintInASlowHand, overmodulatedChyron, bentFontRom, thePictureInTheType, wanderingInset.

## Signal (source A)

invert  (invert (polarity swap))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Negates the composite waveform coming out of the encoder, as if the video pair were wired backwards. At 1 the picture is a full negative. Halfway is the solarized midpoint, where bright and dark both fold toward grey. Hue inverts too, because the colour subcarrier is on the same wire.

deint  (deinterlace)
  0=off 1=on  default 0
  Rebuilds each frame from a single field instead of both, like a bob deinterlacer. Use it when an interlaced source (a captured video or webcam) shows comb teeth on horizontal motion. It costs half the vertical detail, which is the same trade a real deinterlacer makes.

capLumaMHz  (capture luma band (0 off))
  0..4.2 step 0.1 MHz  default 0
  The file was digitised from a tape, and the deck that played it passed only this much luma bandwidth to the capture card. VHS manages about 3 MHz at SP, less at EP, and a camcorder on a worn head under 2. Everything the chain does from here acts on a picture that was already soft, like a tape dubbed from a tape. 0 means the file never went through a deck.

capChromaMHz  (capture chroma band (0 off))
  0..1.5 step 0.05 MHz  default 0
  The colour bandwidth the same deck passed to the capture card. Colour-under records chroma on a 629 kHz carrier, so a home deck passes about 0.5 MHz of it against 3 MHz of luma. Colour smears sideways across many pixels while the edges under it stay sharp. That smear is in the file, so colour-under in the chain here stacks on top of it, as a second deck would.

capNoiseIre  (capture grain)
  0..30 step 0.5 IRE  default 0
  The noise floor of the deck's luma FM path as the capture card saw it: fine grain in every frame of the file. It holds still with the picture when the deck is paused, because it was on the tape rather than in the chain.

capChromaNoiseIre  (capture chroma noise)
  0..60 step 1 IRE  default 0
  Noise on the deck's colour-under carrier, which had a fraction of the luma path's headroom. It reaches the file through the narrow chroma band above, so it arrives as slow blotches of wrong hue and saturation rather than speckle. Lower the capture chroma band to make it blotchier.

capYcDelayNs  (capture y/c delay)
  -500..500 step 10 ns  default 0
  The deck's chroma path arriving at the capture card late (+) or early (-) relative to its luma. Colour is displaced off the edges it belongs to, by a few hundred nanoseconds on a home deck. One sample is 70 ns.

vbi  (vbi test signals)
  0=off 1=on  default 1
  Vertical blanking interval

          - **lines 17-18**: VITS multiburst and a modulated staircase, the
            transmission-test signals engineers measured the plant with.
          - **line 19**: a VIR reference.
          - **line 21**: caption data, a clock run-in and dashes that change
            every frame, because captions are live.

          Invisible in normal framing. Roll the picture or shrink v size and all
          of this appears in the black bar. On by default because a broadcast
          signal carried it. Switch it off for a bare studio feed.

## Noise source (static)

srcNoiseBwMHz  (noise bandwidth)
  0.2..7 step 0.05 MHz  default 4.2
  The bandwidth of the path the noise came through, which sets the grain size: noise cannot change faster than the circuit carrying it allows. A tuner's IF stops at 4.2 MHz, so broadcast snow is fine but not infinitely fine. Per-pixel noise is sharper than any real receiver could produce. Lower it and the grain coarsens into the smeared streaks of a deck reading blank tape, because a playback head's aperture is a second bandwidth limit in series with this one. Less bandwidth also means less noise power, so the field dims as it coarsens. That is the physics rather than something to compensate for.

srcNoiseLevel  (noise power)
  0..2 step 0.01  default 1
  How much noise the detector receives. On an untuned channel this scales the snow against a black floor, because an envelope detector with no carrier has nothing to lift the dark end off zero. On blank tape it scales the swing around mid grey instead, since the deemphasis network still sets the DC level whatever the demodulator does. Past 1 the field clips, which a real front end would only reach with the AGC fully open.

srcNoiseLine  (per-sweep level error)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.15
  A gain error that lasts exactly one scan line: the tuner's AGC hunting on the noise it is trying to measure, or a playback head's contact varying from sweep to sweep. It multiplies rather than adds, so it shows on the noise it is amplifying, and because a sweep is a whole line the result is flickering horizontal bands. This is the difference between snow and the shifting striped texture of blank tape. At zero every line is independent and the field is flat fuzz.

srcNoiseHz  (field refresh)
  1..60 step 0.5 Hz  default 60
  How often the noise field changes. At 60 it changes at display rate, like a live signal. Below that the source delivers fields more slowly than the set draws them, so each one is held for several frames and the boil goes chunky. Non-integer ratios hold fields unevenly, with the same cadence as 3:2 pulldown, from the same arithmetic. A held field is noise with a visible frame rate, and everything downstream carries it: the mixer loop builds structure out of a field that stays still long enough to feed back.

## Video synth (source)

synthAHz  (osc A)
  0..8000000 step 1 Hz  default 15834
  The first oscillator's frequency. What it draws depends on where it sits relative to the raster. At 60 Hz it fits one cycle down the frame and reads as a vertical gradient. At 15734 Hz, the line rate, it fits one cycle across a line and the gradient turns sideways. On an exact multiple it paints that many standing bars. A few hertz off, every line starts the wave a little later than the last, so the bars lean and creep, and the error sets how fast. At 3579545 Hz it lands on the colour subcarrier, so the encoder downstream reads the whole screen as chroma and returns flat colour. Detune from there and hue turns across the picture.

synthBHz  (osc B)
  0..8000000 step 1 Hz  default 60
  The second oscillator, on the same scale. It does nothing until the combiner is off "osc A alone". Then it beats against the first: two free-running oscillators put their difference frequency on screen, so a pair a few hertz apart draws a moire that drifts at the gap between them rather than at either knob.

synthShape  (waveform)
  0=ramp 1=triangle 2=sine 3=pulse  default 2
  The waveform selector, for both oscillators at once. Ramp is the one to try first: a sawtooth is what a ramp generator makes, so at low frequencies it is a clean gradient and at high ones a stack of hard edges. Triangle folds it symmetric. Sine rounds it into something the encoder passes without ringing. Pulse is a comparator output: two levels, hard edges, and the most bandwidth for the rest of the chain to distort.

synthMix  (combiner)
  0=osc A 1=sum 2=ring mod 3=comparator  default 0
  How the two oscillators are combined. Sum is a mixing amplifier driven into its rails, so the two patterns lie over each other and clip where they agree. Ring mod is a balanced multiply, with both carriers suppressed and only their sum and difference left, which is where plaid and moire come from. Comparator puts oscillator B on the reference input of a slicer, so A comes out two-level with its duty cycle modulated wherever the two cross.

synthLevel  (level)
  0..4 step 0.01 x  default 1
  Output contrast around mid-video, before the colorizer. Past 1 the waveform runs into its rails and the shape squares off, so a sine becomes a pulse with soft corners. This makes it a coarse waveshaper too.

synthColor  (colorizer)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  One signal into three guns through three phase shifts 120 degrees apart, which is all a colorizer ever was. At 0 the three agree and the pattern comes out grey. Opened up, signal level becomes hue, so a ramp turns through the whole wheel and a pulse lands on two opposite colours.

synthHueDeg  (colorizer phase)
  0..360 step 1 deg  default 0
  Rotates all three phase shifts together, which slides the whole palette around the wheel without changing how the pattern is coloured. Modulate it and the picture cycles colour while the geometry holds still.

synthColorSoftPx  (colorizer input filter)
  0..24 step 0.1 px  default 0
  The lowpass a colorizer box has ahead of its slicers, which decides how large the colour fields are. A slicer given a sharp picture finds a threshold crossing on every piece of detail and posterizes into confetti. Given a soft one it finds a few long boundaries and the picture comes out in slabs. It filters only the colorizer's input. The picture that reaches the screen keeps all its own detail, so the result is a sharp image with flat colour on it. It filters both axes, unlike the capture band above it, which is a tape loss and so horizontal only.

synthColorSrc  (colorizer input)
  0=oscillator 1=picture  default 0
  What the colorizer is slicing. Its own oscillator is one input. The picture is the other, and that is how a colorizer box was actually sold: video in, colour out, with the oscillators out of circuit. Pointed at the picture it turns the image's own brightness into hue, so two areas at the same brightness come back the same colour however far apart they are on screen. That is what lays colour down in large fields: an encoder puts colour on detail, and this puts it on tone. Needs the synth over a picture to have anything to read, since a synth patched in as a source has nothing in front of it.

synthColorMode  (colorizer type)
  0=phase shifts 1=comparators  default 0
  How the box turns level into colour. Phase shifts sends one signal into three guns through three shifts 120 degrees apart, so level turns continuously through the wheel and a gradient comes back as a smooth sweep of hue. Comparators is how the cheap boxes did it before anyone put a phase shifter in one: three slicers at three different levels, each gun switched fully on or off at its own threshold. The output can then only be one of eight corners of the colour cube, so the picture is posterized into flat areas of saturated primary with hard edges between them. The hue knob slides the three thresholds together to move those edges through the tonal range.

synthOver  (over picture (A))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Lays the synth over slot A's picture rather than replacing it, so it becomes a module in the chain instead of a source. Source A only: slot B's pass writes its texture rather than reading one, so there is no picture on that side to lay anything over. Does nothing while A is already showing the synth, because then the synth is the picture.

synthFm  (luma → osc A)
  0..200000 step 10 Hz  default 0
  The picture's own brightness into oscillator A's frequency input, the patch every video synth was bought for. It pulls the frequency rather than offsetting the phase, so the wave genuinely runs faster through bright picture and slower through dark. The spacing of the bars becomes the brightness, and equal-brightness regions fall into step, so the image draws itself as contour lines. Needs something over the picture to read, so it does nothing until the control above is up.

synthFmSrc  (that input, patched to)
  0=the deck 1=the loop  default 0
  Which picture the frequency input reads. The deck is the slot's own, so the contours land on the source and are redrawn from scratch every frame. The loop is the camera's return, the picture this stage wrote a frame ago with the synth already in it. The contours are then traced on the last generation's contours and the result goes round again: the frequency at a point is set by how bright the oscillator's own drawing was there last time. Nothing in the patch decides what that settles into, and it does not settle. With the camera loop out it reads the same picture the deck does, since there is no return to read.

## Feed A · deck

aPause  (A pause (deck held))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The pause button on the deck feeding input A, at how badly the deck copes with it. The frame holds, because the drum keeps re-reading one track, but pause defeats the capstan servo. Every line of the program's own signal scatters sideways around a slow wander, the raster hops when the servo hunts vertically, and a mistrack stripe of snow creeps through the picture. A is the house reference, so the receiver's PLL hunts on every line and hue wobbles with the displacement. If B is up, B's clean sync starts winning sync contests it used to lose.

aDropoutRate  (A dropouts)
  0..400 step 1 /frame  default 0
  Dropout events per frame on the tape feeding input A alone. Shed oxide means the head reads nothing for a moment and the detector outputs snow. This feed has no delay-line compensator, so every gap stays a raw streak. B sums in over the scars untouched.

aDropoutLenUs  (A dropout len)
  1..60 step 0.5 us  default 5
  How long each of A's dropouts lasts, in microseconds of the 63.5 µs line.

aScramble  (A sync suppression)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Head-end scrambling on input A alone. A premium channel is scrambled per channel, not per set. A's sync tips are lifted toward blanking before the mix, so the receiver has to choose between A's damaged pulses and whatever B is offering. Mixing in a little clean B is the pirate trick of feeding a decoder substitute sync.

aScrambleMode  (A system)
  0=gated 1=alternate 2=ssavi  default 0
  Which scrambling system A's channel uses. Gated suppresses every line, alternate every other line, and SSAVI also inverts the active video, so A leaks through as a negative while B stays positive.

## Feed A · cable

aConnector  (A loose connector)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How loose the plug in input A's jack is. Bands of lines lose contact, re-rolled every frame, the way a plug hanging on its own cable weight makes and breaks. Which contact is failing is the row below, and on a per-input feed that choice matters more than on the program bus: a break that takes A's sync leaves the receiver B's pulses to lock to.

aConnectorMode  (A bad contact)
  0=pin 1=shield 2=both  default 0
  Which of A's two contacts is intermittent. The centre pin breaks the signal path, so those bands collapse to the input's own noise and take A's sync tips with them. With B patched in, the receiver locks to B's pulses for the length of the band and returns to A's line start when contact comes back, so the picture snaps between two geometries. The shell breaks the ground reference instead and leaves the signal alone: the return current runs through the mains earth, so a ground loop's hum lands on the bad bands and A's level walks and buzzes while its picture and sync survive. Both is a wiggled plug, with the two faults on independent bands.

aHumIre  (A ground loop)
  -40..40 step 0.5 IRE  default 0
  A ground loop on input A's cable alone. A loop needs two earthed boxes joined by a shield, so it belongs to one run, this deck's outlet against the mixer's. That is why a hum bar on the program bus cannot say which cable carries it and this can. It lifts A's sync tips along with A's picture, so the receiver's AGC and hold chase A sixty times a second while B sits still. Which of the two wins the sync contest alternates with the hum phase, so the picture rolls with the bar instead of just wearing it. Negative is the other leg of a split-phase service, the same bar 180° round, so two feeds on opposite legs push against each other rather than together.

aNoiseIre  (A noise)
  0..150 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  Snow on A's feed only, from a long antenna run or a bad patch cable ahead of the mixer. B sums in clean over the top, which is what tells a noisy input apart from a noisy program bus.

aTermination  (A termination (-1 daisy, +1 open))
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Termination fault on A's cable alone. Negative is double-terminated: A arrives dim and shallow, so it loses the sync contest against a healthy B. Positive is unterminated: A runs hot and rings with a short reflection echo while B stays clean.

aPolarity  (A polarity (flips sync))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A signal/ground swap on A's own connector. A's waveform is negated, sync included, before it reaches the mixer. Unlike pulling A gain negative this holds even when the mixer path is idle, and unlike the program-bus polarity swap it leaves B's signal and sync untouched, so the receiver may latch onto B instead.

## Camera feedback (optical)

fbMix  (mix)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How much of the camera-pointed-at-the-monitor image is fed back into the input. This is the classic video feedback loop, and it is half of the round trip: the fader and the exposure below multiply, so a mix of 0.6 costs the loop 40 percent per lap, which no exposure under 1.67 makes back. Raise the two together until the product passes unity and the picture starts building structure on its own. Everything below shapes what the loop does on each trip around.

fbZoom  (zoom)
  0.2..4 step 0.001 x  default 1.05
  How much bigger or smaller the camera frames the screen each time around. Above 1 detail flows outward and tunnels form. Below 1 it collapses inward. The distance from 1 sets how fast the loop moves, and tiny offsets are usually the most interesting.

fbRotateDeg  (rotate)
  -180..180 step 0.01 deg  default 0
  Camera tilt on the loop. Each pass rotates the image again, so structures spiral instead of expanding straight out. Combined with zoom this gives the classic logarithmic-spiral feedback. A hundredth of a degree visibly changes how fast the spiral winds, which is why the track is fine around zero and coarse at the ends.

fbShiftX  (shift x)
  -1..1 step 0.001  default 0
  Camera aim off-centre horizontally. Moves the feedback fixed point, which decides where the tunnel mouth or spiral core lands on screen.

fbShiftY  (shift y)
  -1..1 step 0.001  default 0
  Camera aim off-centre vertically. Same as shift x on the other axis. Together they steer the centre of the loop.

fbGain  (gain)
  0..3 step 0.001 x  default 1
  Camera exposure on the loop. The round trip gain is this times the mix above. At a mix of 0.6 the threshold where patterns persist is an exposure of 1.67, and below it the loop is a smear a few frames deep however far past 1 the exposure reads. Which side of that threshold is safe depends on the zoom: a loop collapsing inward concentrates its gain into a shrinking core and holds a picture well above unity, while one expanding outward spreads it over the whole raster and goes to white within a second of crossing.

fbIris  (auto-iris hunt)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Puts the camera's exposure on its own auto-iris servo instead of the fixed gain above. The camera is metering the monitor it feeds, so the servo is inside the loop it is trying to steady: the loop brightens, the iris clamps a beat later, the loop starves, the iris reopens. Turned up, the mechanical lag outruns the damping and it never settles: bloom, clamp, collapse, reopen, at the servo's own rhythm. It runs at a different natural frequency from the beam limiter (in Deflection), so with both engaged the two beat against each other.

fbFocus  (defocus)
  0..12 step 0.05 px  default 0.7
  Lens blur radius on the camera. A little defocus keeps a feedback loop from going straight to pixel noise. It smooths each generation, so the loop favours large soft structures over single-pixel speckle.

fbVign  (vignette)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.2
  Lens falloff toward the corners. Loop gain becomes position-dependent, high in the middle and low at the edges, so feedback lives in the centre of frame and dies before it reaches the border.

fbBlack  (black cut)
  0..0.2 step 0.005  default 0.03
  The camera sensor's black level. Anything dimmer than this reads as pure black, so trails do not linger forever at low level. They thin and cut off once they fall under the threshold.

fbKnee  (cam s-curve)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.35
  Sensor highlight compression. Bright areas roll off into a shoulder instead of clipping flat, which turns a runaway loop into thick glowing bands rather than a white-out.

## Tube face (what the camera shoots)

crtCutoff  (beam cutoff)
  0..0.95 step 0.01  default 0
  The gun bias point. Drive below this emits no light at all. It gives the tube a true black background and, in a feedback loop, sets the floor everything has to stay above to survive another pass.

crtGamma  (beam gamma)
  0.2..6 step 0.05  default 1
  The gun transfer curve, light out versus drive in. High gamma deepens shadows and stretches highlights, which is much of what gives a CRT its contrast. In a feedback loop it sharpens the boundary between what survives and what dies.

crtSat  (beam saturation)
  0..6 step 0.01  default 1
  Colour saturation of the emitted light, applied after the beam transfer. Feedback multiplies it every pass, so a small boost here compounds into heavily saturated bands.

crtBloom  (screen bloom)
  0..6 step 0.01  default 0.2
  Light spreading out of bright phosphor cores. A tight halo that fattens highlights. In a loop, it is how a bright point grows into a blob over successive passes.

crtHalation  (halation (warm halo))
  0..6 step 0.01  default 0.15
  Light scattering inside the thick glass faceplate and bouncing back: a wide, warm, low-level halo around highlights. Broader and softer than bloom, and the reason bright CRT images look like they glow through the screen rather than off it.

crtHaloKey  (halation ∝ beam current)
  0..4 step 0.01  default 0.8
  How much the halo widens with local beam drive. At 0 the halo is one fixed width, which is the giveaway. Real glass scatter grows with beam current, so a peak white throws light much further into the faceplate than a mid grey. Raise it and highlights bloom disproportionately while ordinary picture keeps a tight halo.

crtGlow  (phosphor glow)
  0..4 step 0.01  default 0.08
  Faceplate haze: the dull ambient sheen a powered tube has even in black areas. It lifts the black floor slightly, which in a feedback loop gives the whole frame a small standing gain.

## Mixer feedback (electrical)

cfbMix  (loop mix)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Feedback through a video mixer instead of a camera. The previous frame's composite waveform is patched back into the input electrically, and this is the crossfader position toward that loop bus. The subcarrier goes around the loop too, so colour does things optics cannot. All the way over, the crossfader is past the loop bus rather than on it: the program is fully out, so the loop has only itself to feed on, and the delay and filters take a little off every lap. Below unity gain that decays to black in about a second. It stays a picture only if the loop makes back what it loses, which is what the gain beside it is for.

cfbGain  (loop gain)
  -3..3 step 0.01 x  default 1
  Proc-amp trim on the loop return. Past ±1 the round trip exceeds unity and the loop builds until it clips. Negative inverts each pass, so the picture alternates polarity frame to frame and edges buzz.

cfbDelayUs  (loop delay)
  0..63 step 0.001 us  default 0.15
  Delay on the loop return, in microseconds. Because the colour subcarrier rides the same waveform, delay is also a hue rotation: one sample (70 ns) is a 90° spin. Sub-microsecond moves smear the picture sideways and recolour it at the same time.

cfbServoUs  (loop timebase pull)
  -60..60 step 0.01 us  default 0
  The loop's delay trimmer replaced by a varactor hanging off the video bus, so the fed-back waveform tunes the delay it passes through. Bright content and sync tips pull opposite ways from mid-video, and every 70 ns of pull is another 90° of hue. Each lap the picture rewrites its own timing and colour, and that rewritten picture does the pulling on the next lap. Structures shear apart by brightness, sync walks into neighbouring lines and tears, and none of it repeats, because the displacement field is the picture itself one generation late. Sign chooses which way brightness pulls.

cfbLines  (v offset)
  -240..240 step 1 lines  default 0
  Vertical offset applied each trip around the loop. Every generation slides a few lines up or down, so trails walk vertically and stack into ladders instead of sitting still.

cfbKey  (loop key)
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Keys the loop return, so only part of the picture feeds back. Positive keeps the side of the slice the key is set to. Negative inverts the polarity and keeps the other. This is what makes feedback follow the subject instead of flooding the frame. The box slices the level below, until the acceptance angle opens and it slices hue instead.

cfbKeyLevel  (key level)
  0..100 step 0.5 IRE  default 45
  The brightness the loop key slices at, in IRE (0 is blanking, 100 is peak white). Sets where the boundary between fed-back and not falls.

cfbKeySoft  (key soft)
  1..30 step 0.5 IRE  default 8
  How wide the key transition is, in IRE. Narrow gives a hard-edged cut-out. Wide gives a gradual blend that follows the picture gradient.

cfbKeyExt  (key input)
  0=self 1=program  default 0
  Which connector the keyer's key input is on. Self is the loop return itself, so the loop's own past decides where it may continue: the trail draws its own boundary, and the boundary is a generation old. Program is the live picture, so what decides is what is in front of the camera now. A subject moving through the frame carves its own shape out of everything the loop has accumulated, and the accumulation cannot follow it.

cfbKeyHueDeg  (key hue)
  0..360 step 1 deg  default 180
  Which chroma phase the keyer slices at, once the acceptance angle below has switched it from level to hue. 241 is where a green backing lands. In a loop the number matters less than where it sits relative to the hue the delay is spinning the return through.

cfbKeyAcceptDeg  (key acceptance)
  0..180 step 1 deg  default 0
  Swaps the luma keyer in the loop for a chroma one: a wedge this wide either side of the key hue. At zero there is no wedge and the box goes back to slicing level. A loop keyed on its own colour is self-limiting, because the loop delay is a hue rotation. A region regenerates until its own return has spun out of the wedge, then stops, and whatever has spun into the wedge takes over. Nothing draws the boundary and nothing holds it still.

cfbHold  (strobe hold)
  0..60 step 1 frames  default 0
  Freezes the loop's frame store for this many frames before it grabs again, like a frame synchronizer stuttering. At small values motion strobes. At large ones the picture holds still while the live signal keeps mixing over it.

cfbTrail  (trails)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Peak-hold decay in the loop's frame store. Bright areas are retained and fade rather than being replaced. This is the smeared luminance trail of a frame synchronizer left in the loop, distinct from the tube's own phosphor persistence.

cfbFilterMHz  (loop resonance freq (0 off))
  0..5 step 0.05 MHz  default 0
  Puts a resonant filter in the loop, centred here, like a bent video enhancer patched into the feedback. Around 3.58 MHz it rings on the colour subcarrier itself. Lower down it rings on picture detail and turns edges into repeating bars.

cfbFilterQ  (loop resonance Q (broad→ringing))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.5
  How selective that resonance is. Broad gives the loop a gentle tonal tilt. Narrow makes it ring for a long time after every edge, laying a fixed-frequency pattern across the line.

cfbFilterBoost  (loop resonance boost)
  0..16 step 0.05 x  default 2
  In-band gain added by the resonance. Push it far enough that the round trip exceeds unity at that frequency and the loop self-oscillates: the filter starts generating its own pattern out of nothing.

cfbRing  (loop ring mod)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The loop bus multiplied instead of summed with what it meets: a ring modulator with one input patched to the machine's own past. Every product goes round again and is re-multiplied a frame later, so the spectrum folds over itself generation after generation. What is on the other input is the row below, and it decides whether any of that arrives as colour.

cfbClockPct  (read clock error)
  -2..2 step 0.001 %  default 0
  The loop's frame store read out at a clock this far off the one it was written at. A store re-triggers its readout on the output's line sync, so the error starts again every line rather than accumulating down the frame. The picture is stretched or squeezed sideways from the line start, and past the end of a line the read runs into the store's next one. It is a colour control because the subcarrier is in the samples being re-clocked. A thousandth off, and the carrier comes back a thousandth off the lattice the decoder measures against, so hue turns further the further a sample sits from the line start: eighty degrees by the right-hand edge. Each lap re-clocks what the last one wrote, so the fan opens wider every generation. Neither a lens nor a delay can do this. Both move a picture without changing where its carrier sits.

cfbGenlock  (frame sync on the return)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Whether the return comes back through a frame synchronizer or down a bare cable. A store genlocked to house reference writes its own sync and burst on the way out, so what circulates is picture only. The delay, the offsets and the varactor can be run as far as they go and the receiver still finds every line start, which is what lets a loop be pushed hard and stay a picture. On the cable the loop's own sync tip goes round with the video, one delay late, and lands somewhere inside a line. The separator loses the edge it was looking for, the flywheel free-runs, and a second's worth of accumulated structure is thrown across a raster that no longer lines up with it. Both are things a rack does. This is which one is patched.

cfbReturn  (return (Y/C split))
  0=composite 1=chroma 2=luma  default 0
  A Y/C separator on the loop return and a recombiner after it, so one wire comes round the loop and the other comes from the live picture. Composite sends the whole waveform round, which is what a loop normally is. Chroma sends the loop's colour over the live brightness. Hue accumulates and keeps turning through the delay's rotation while the picture under it stays sharp and current, so what builds up is colour detached from the thing that cast it. Luma is the reverse: brightness and the sync tip go round underneath the live colour, so trails stack up in grey and still pull at where the receiver thinks each line starts.

cfbRingSrc  (ring carrier)
  0=program 1=oscillator  default 0
  Which connector the ring modulator's other input is on. Program is the live picture, and both sides then carry their subcarrier on the same crystal. Chroma against chroma lands at DC and at 7.16 MHz, the chroma filter keeps neither, and what the multiply produces is brightness structure and pulses created mid-line. Oscillator patches the box's own subcarrier generator there instead, which makes the bridge an encoder's chroma modulator. The return's brightness is translated up onto 3.58 MHz, where the decoder reads it as colour, and the return's colour is translated down to brightness. Each lap swaps the two, so a picture's light comes back as its hue and that hue comes back as light.

cfbCarrierKHz  (ring carrier detune)
  -200..200 step 0.01 kHz  default 0
  How far that oscillator sits off the house 3.579545 MHz. At zero it agrees with the encoder, so the colour it makes out of brightness lands on one phase and the picture comes back in a single hue. Detuned, the phase it writes with ramps continuously through the frame, so the manufactured colour turns along every line and down the picture, faster the further off it is. It is a second crystal in a second box, so nothing pulls it back. The hue keeps turning as long as it runs.

## A/B Mixer

bGenlock  (genlock)
  0=dirty sum 1=clean dissolve  default 0
  Whether source B is genlocked to the house reference. Off (0): B free-runs and is summed into the composite, a wiring fault, so its detune, roll and skew below produce fighting sync and chroma beats. On (1): B is re-encoded on A's carrier and raster and the combine becomes a clean crossfade, a production switcher dissolve, with B gain as the fader and the wipe as a clean B-replaces-A wipe. The detune, roll, skew and ring mod do nothing on this path.

aGain  (A gain)
  -3..3 step 0.01 x  default 1
  A's own level on the summing bus (dirty path only). 1 is full program. Pull it down to fade A out under B for a manual crossfade, or take it negative to invert A into a difference key that cancels against B. Does nothing on the genlocked clean-dissolve path, where A is implied by (1 − B gain).

bGain  (B gain)
  -3..3 step 0.01 x  default 0
  How much of source B reaches the composite line. With genlock off this is the level B is summed in at, a wiring fault rather than a clean dissolve, and negative inverts B's whole signal, sync tips included, the same polarity trick as A gain. With genlock on it is the crossfade fader: 0 full A, 1 full B, and anything below 0 is a closed fader, since a dissolve has nothing to invert. Everything below detunes B's timebase relative to A (dirty path only).

bRing  (ring mod)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Multiplies the two composite signals instead of adding them. The product of two subcarriers lands at sum and difference frequencies, so the picture comes back in colours neither source contained.

busClip  (bus overload)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How little headroom the summing amplifier has. Two full composites added is twice the amplitude one was designed to carry, and at 0 the sum goes into the channel as pure arithmetic, a bus that never runs into its supply. Open it and the stage runs out of volts: its gain falls away toward the rail rather than clipping flat, and a falling gain multiplies the two signals sharing the bus by each other. A detuned B then beats against A and lands products at their difference, inside the chroma band, so colour arrives that neither source carries. This is what the ring mod beside it does deliberately, happening because the box ran out of volts. Sync tips are squashed with everything else, so the sync contest changes too: a deeper tip wins by less once both are against the rail.

bLineHz  (line offset)
  -60..60 step 0.01 Hz  default 0.15
  How far B's line rate sits from A's. B slides sideways continuously, skewing a little more on each successive line, because the two horizontal oscillators are not locked. At zero it stops but stays where it drifted to.

bDetuneHz  (sc detune)
  -3000..3000 step 0.01 Hz  default 40
  How far B's colour subcarrier sits from A's 3.579545 MHz. The decoder locks to A's burst, so B's colour beats against it and its hue cycles continuously: the rainbow crawl of a non-genlocked source.

bRollLps  (frame roll)
  -30..30 step 0.01 l/f  default 0.1
  B's vertical drift in lines per frame, from its field rate not matching A's. B creeps up or down through the frame independently of the picture A is painting.

## Signal (source B)

bHueDeg  (B hue)
  -180..180 step 1 deg  default 0
  Proc-amp hue trim on B before it is mixed: a static phase offset on its subcarrier. Unlike sc detune this does not drift. It just parks B's colours somewhere else.

bVidGain  (B video gain)
  0..6 step 0.01 x  default 1
  Proc-amp video gain on B: contrast of the B picture before mixing, without changing how much of B is patched in.

bInv  (B invert)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Inverts B's picture. Mixed against A this reads as a difference key. Where the two agree they cancel toward flat grey, and where they differ the mix lights up.

deintB  (B deinterlace)
  0=off 1=on  default 0
  The same bob deinterlacer source A has, on B's own picture: each frame rebuilt from one field instead of both, at half the vertical detail. B is where the second grabber goes, and a deck's combing is its own. A progressive camera in A and an interlaced dongle in B want opposite answers, which is why this is a switch per source rather than one on the bus.

## Feed B · deck

bPause  (B pause (deck held))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The pause button on the B deck, at how badly the deck copes with it. The frame holds, because the drum keeps re-reading one track, but pause defeats the capstan servo. B's timebase wanders aperiodically and scatters line to line. The head sweeps off the parked track through a mistrack stripe of snow that creeps down the frame on its own. The drum's two reads never had their colour-under phase interleaved, so B's hue flickers at frame rate. All of it lands on B's own raster and then rides the dirty sum, which is the classic rig: a paused VCR into a mixer, two fighting syncs, one of them broken. When the stripe drifts through B's vertical interval it takes B's field pulses with it and the fight turns into unplanned rolls. Genlock implies a time-base corrector, so on the clean-dissolve path the button just freezes the frame.

bDropoutRate  (B dropouts)
  0..400 step 1 /frame  default 0
  Dropout events per frame on B's own tape. The streaks land on B's raster, so they slip, skew and roll with B's picture through the mix. That is what tells B's worn tape apart from damage on the program bus.

bDropoutLenUs  (B dropout len)
  1..60 step 0.5 us  default 5
  How long each of B's dropouts lasts, in microseconds of the 63.5 µs line.

bScramble  (B sync suppression)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Head-end scrambling on input B alone. B's sync tips are lifted toward blanking before it is summed in. B stops contributing to the sync contest: its picture still beats and rolls through the mix, but the receiver only ever sees A's pulses.

bScrambleMode  (B system)
  0=gated 1=alternate 2=ssavi  default 0
  Which scrambling system B's channel uses. Gated suppresses every line, alternate every other line, and SSAVI also inverts B's active video: a negative picture drifting through a positive one.

## Feed B · cable

bConnector  (B loose connector)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How loose the plug in input B's jack is. Bands of lines lose contact, re-rolled every frame. Which contact is failing is the row below. B is the input the receiver is not locked to, so a break here decides whether B's bands stop contributing picture or stop contributing sync, which are two different fights.

bConnectorMode  (B bad contact)
  0=pin 1=shield 2=both  default 0
  Which of B's two contacts is intermittent. The centre pin breaks the signal path, so those bands of B collapse to the input's own noise and B stops pushing sync there. The mix goes quiet and steady for a band, then B's pulses come back and the fight resumes. The shell breaks the ground instead and leaves B's signal alone: a ground loop's hum lands on the bad bands, so B arrives on a shifting pedestal that rides B's own raster through the slip and roll. Both is a wiggled plug, with the two faults on independent bands.

bHumIre  (B ground loop)
  -40..40 step 0.5 IRE  default 0
  A ground loop on input B's cable alone: B's deck and the mixer on different outlets, with the loop current in series with B's video. The bar rides B's own raster, so unlike a program-bus hum it slips and rolls with B's picture instead of standing still on the glass. It lifts B's sync tips with it, so how hard B fights for the line start varies at 60 Hz. Negative is the other leg of the mains. Set against A's ground loop it pushes the opposite way, which is the difference between two hum bars that agree and two that beat.

bNoiseIre  (B noise)
  0..150 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  Snow on B's feed only. It rides B's own raster through the slip and roll, so the noise tears and rolls with B's picture instead of sitting still on the screen the way program-bus noise does.

bTermination  (B termination (-1 daisy, +1 open))
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Termination fault on B's cable alone. Negative halves B toward a dim ghost of a signal under A. Positive runs B hot and ringing, so its sync and burst push harder in the contest against a clean A.

bPolarity  (B polarity (flips sync))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A signal/ground swap on B's own connector. B's waveform is negated, sync included, before it reaches the summing bus. The same trick as pulling B gain negative, but as a fault in the cable rather than the fader, so level and polarity stay independent knobs.

## Character generator (chyron)

cgMix  (cg over program)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A character generator at the switcher, keying the caption text
          into the picture, the box every lower third, score bug and station
          ident came out of.

          What makes it a CG rather than an overlay is that it puts out **two
          wires**: a fill, which is video, and a key, which is a matte cut at
          the characters' own edges. Everything below changes the relationship
          between those two, which is what every bent chyron is doing.

          Because it keys onto the composite bus ahead of the loops and the
          deck, what it writes is signal from here on. Full-swing type is the
          harshest thing a composite path carries, so the AGC pumps on it, the
          sound detector turns it into a whine that changes with the text, and
          the tape ages it along with the picture.

cgKeyDelayNs  (key timing)
  -600..600 step 10 ns  default 0
  The trim every real keyer has, because the key path and the video path are different lengths of circuit. Mis-set on a photograph it slides a soft matte a few samples and nobody notices. Mis-set on a glyph it puts background through one side of every stem and a hard shadow down the other, and far enough out it leaves an outline with no letter inside it. One sample is 70 ns.

cgClip  (key clip)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.5
  Where the slicer cuts the processed key. On type this is stroke weight rather than an edge position. Down, thin strokes fuse and the whole line grows a halo. Up, stems drop out of the middle of words. How much range it has depends on the key bandwidth below: a key with no soft edge has nothing for a clip to slide along.

cgKeyMHz  (key bandwidth)
  0.3..8 step 0.1 MHz  default 3
  The key-processing amplifier ahead of the slicer, which is narrower than the video path and is the only reason a key has a soft edge at all. Horizontal only, the same lopsided edge the chroma keyer has, for the same reason: this is a line of signal rather than a picture, so there is no vertical neighbour on the wire.

cgInvert  (key invert)
  0=normal 1=inverted  default 0
  Which side of the key is cut. Inverted, the box fills the whole raster and the letters are holes in it showing the picture. That is what a downstream keyer inverted actually does, since the key's domain is the picture rather than the block of type.

cgEdgeX  (edge offset x)
  -24..24 step 1 smp  default 0
  A CG drew its border and drop shadow by delaying the key a sample and a line and OR-ing it back in underneath the fill. This is that delay. Pulling it far past the sample it was meant to be detaches the shadow from the type and moves it across the frame.

cgEdgeY  (edge offset y)
  -24..24 step 1 ln  default 0
  The other half of the drop shadow, in lines. Bending the two apart puts a shadow in front of the letters it belongs to instead of behind them.

cgFill  (fill level)
  0..120 step 1 IRE  default 100
  How bright the characters are laid in, in IRE on the composite. 100 is peak white. Past that the box is overmodulating, and everything downstream that reacts to level reacts to it: the receiver AGC, the tape, and the sound detector, which starts buzzing in time with the caption.

cgX  (cg x)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.08
  The block's left edge across the picture.

cgY  (cg y)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.52
  The block's top edge down the picture. The stock value is a lower third, clear of the caption decoder's own block below it. The two are meant to be run together and compared.

cgScale  (cg size)
  1..6 step 0.25  default 2
  Picture samples per font dot. The glyphs are dots on a grid, so this scales in whole dots and the type stays as blocky as the ROM made it.

cgRomAddr  (cg rom address line)
  0..11 step 1  default 0
  A pin held high on this box's font ROM. The same bend as the caption decoder's, on a different chip, because these are two boxes and shorting one says nothing about the other. Low lines carry the row inside the cell, so every glyph grows a seam. High lines carry the character code, so the whole font is substituted.

cgRomData  (cg rom data line)
  -8..8 step 1  default 0
  The data bus of the same chip: eight dots across one row, so holding one stripes a column down every character on the page. Positive holds it high, negative holds it low.

## Wipe (A/B)

wipeMode  (pattern)
  0=off 1=h 2=v 3=box 4=diamond  default 0
  Selects the switcher wipe pattern that decides which parts of the frame show B instead of A: 0 off, 1 horizontal, 2 vertical, 3 box, 4 diamond. The pattern shapes the picture only. On the dirty path B's sync and burst keep summing across the whole raster whatever the wipe does, so a wipe changes what you see without stopping the sync contest underneath it.

wipePos  (position)
  0..1 step 0.001  default 0.5
  The wipe lever: where the A/B boundary sits, 0 full A to 1 full B.

wipeSoft  (softness)
  0..0.5 step 0.005  default 0.05
  Width of the blended border along the wipe edge. A hard switcher cut at 0, a soft dissolving edge as it opens up.

wipeRate  (sweep)
  0..2 step 0.01 Hz  default 0
  Drives the wipe lever back and forth automatically at this rate, so the boundary sweeps on its own. Can be locked to MIDI clock with the ♩ icon.

## PiP inset (source B)

pipMix  (inset key)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Squeezes source B into a positionable window over the program, like a switcher DVE. Unlike the dirty mix, the inset is re-encoded genlocked to the house raster, so it dot-crawls like real video but does not beat or roll.

pipX  (center x)
  0..1 step 0.005  default 0.72
  Horizontal centre of the inset window across the active picture.

pipY  (center y)
  0..1 step 0.005  default 0.28
  Vertical centre of the inset window down the active picture.

pipW  (width)
  0.1..1 step 0.005  default 0.36
  Width of the inset window, as a fraction of the active picture.

pipH  (height)
  0.1..1 step 0.005  default 0.36
  Height of the inset window, as a fraction of the active picture.

pipBorder  (border)
  0..0.03 step 0.001  default 0.006
  Thickness of the matte border drawn around the inset, the hard frame line a switcher puts around a squeezed source.

pipSoft  (edge soft)
  0..0.05 step 0.001  default 0.004
  Softness of the inset window edge, so the box blends into the program instead of cutting hard.

pipKey  (luma key (- inverts))
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Keys the inset against its own brightness so it is not a solid box. Positive keeps the bright parts of B, negative keeps the dark ones. This is how you drop a subject in without the rectangle.

pipKeyLevel  (key level)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.2
  The brightness the inset key slices at, 0 black to 1 white.

pipKeySoft  (key soft)
  0.01..0.4 step 0.01  default 0.08
  Width of the inset key transition. Narrow cuts a hard matte. Wide feathers the subject into the program.

## Chroma key (A through B)

bKey  (key (- inverts))
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Cuts B's backing colour away so A shows through it: a chroma keyer across the mixer, with B as the foreground. Negative inverts which side survives, so the subject is cut out and the backing kept. Because the keyer is on the bus it slices the chroma the encoder made, not the colour the camera saw, so the matte it cuts is soft across and sharp down, the lopsided edge every composite key had. Narrowing the encoder's chroma bandwidth widens that edge, since it is the same filter.

bKeyHueDeg  (backing hue)
  0..360 step 1 deg  default 241
  Which chroma phase the keyer treats as the backing. 241 is where a pure green screen lands, 347 a blue one. These are angles on the colour wheel the subcarrier carries rather than names, which is why anything sharing a hue with the backing disappears too. Sweeping it live keys through the whole picture in turn.

bKeyAcceptDeg  (acceptance)
  0..180 step 1 deg  default 40
  How wide a wedge of hue either side of the backing counts as backing. Narrow takes only the backing itself and leaves every shadow and fold on it opaque. Wide starts eating anything that leans that way, which on a warm-lit subject is the skin. Past about 90 it is keying half the colour wheel.

bKeyClip  (clip)
  0..0.3 step 0.005  default 0.06
  The saturation a sample must reach before the keyer will act on its hue at all. A demodulator given an unsaturated sample reports an essentially arbitrary phase, so without this the greys and blacks key out at random. It is also why a keyer cannot hold a dark subject against a dark backing: below the clip the two are the same signal.

bKeySoft  (gain (edge))
  0..0.4 step 0.005  default 0.05
  How fast the keyer swings between keep and cut, in both hue and saturation at once, the "gain" knob on the front of the box. At 0 the comparator snaps and the matte is a hard stencil with the composite edge showing as steps. Open it up and the subject feathers into A, taking the backing colour with it unless spill is up.

bKeySpill  (spill kill)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Cancels the backing colour still reflecting off the subject. You cannot lift green off a composite sample, because luma and chroma are the same wire, so the box does what the hardware did and reinjects the backing's own subcarrier in antiphase to null the component along it. It nulls fully on the genlocked path, where B's carrier phase is known exactly. On the dirty path B's carrier is drifting, so the cancellation is always a little late and leaves a residue that varies with the slip.

bKeyDelayUs  (key delay)
  -1.5..1.5 step 0.01 us  default 0
  Where the keyer looks, relative to where the picture it is gating came from: the registration trim, because the key path and the video path are different lengths of circuit. Off zero the matte lies beside the subject instead of over it. One edge keeps a rim of backing colour and the other eats a rim of subject.

bKeyFill  (fill)
  0=program A 1=matte 2=loop bus  default 0
  What shows through the hole the key cut, the connector on the back of a real keyer. Program A is the other input. Matte is the box's own generator, a flat colour encoded on the house carrier, so it dot-crawls and demodulates like any other colour rather than being an RGB value pasted on the output. Loop bus patches the mixer's own last frame into the fill, so the feedback only regenerates inside the keyed shape and grows in the silhouette of whatever was the backing colour. Genlocked path only: a fill sits behind the foreground, and only a crossfade has a behind. On the dirty sum both signals are on the wire at once, so there the key just gates B and A is always present.

bKeyMatteY  (matte level)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.5
  How bright the matte generator sits, black to peak white. This is the luma of a real encoded line, so pushing it to the top with saturation up puts the sum past 100 IRE, and whatever is downstream (the AGC, the tape, the beam limiter) reacts to an over-level signal.

bKeyMatteHueDeg  (matte hue)
  0..360 step 1 deg  default 0
  The matte colour, as a phase on the subcarrier, the same wheel the backing hue above is read off. Setting it near the backing hue is the self-defeating case worth knowing about: the fill lands inside the acceptance wedge, so anything that keys the matte away keys it again next generation through a loop.

bKeyMatteSat  (matte saturation)
  0..0.6 step 0.01  default 0
  How much chroma the matte generator puts on the carrier. At 0 it is a flat grey field with no subcarrier at all, which is the correct way to get a black or white fill. Opened up it approaches the amplitude of a fully saturated primary.

## Recording (luma & FM)

lumaMHz  (luma bandwidth)
  0.3..6 step 0.05 MHz  default 4.2
  How much brightness detail the recording or channel passes. Broadcast is about 4.2 MHz. VHS manages roughly 3 MHz, EP mode less. Lowering it softens fine horizontal detail the way a worn tape does: vertical edges smear while the picture stays sharp top to bottom.

lumaPeak  (peaking)
  0..12 step 0.05  default 0
  The sharpness boost VCRs and TVs apply to fake back the detail the bandwidth limit removed. It overshoots on every edge, laying a bright ringing outline against a dark one: the crispening artifact of consumer video.

diffGain  (differential gain)
  -0.5..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The video amplifier's gain is not flat against the brightness it is amplifying at that instant, so the colour subcarrier riding bright picture comes through smaller than the same colour on dark picture. Saturation drains out of the highlights while the shadows keep theirs. Every VTR and proc amp spec sheet lists this as DG%. Here the full knob wipes chroma off peak white entirely. Negative is the opposite misdesign: colour swells in the brights.

diffPhaseDeg  (differential phase)
  -60..60 step 0.5 deg  default 0
  The same amplifier's delay moves with brightness, and a delay at 3.58 MHz is a phase shift, so hue swings with the luma underneath it. A face turns one way in the light and the other in the shadow, and flat colour picks up an error that tracks the picture. The burst sits at blanking level where the shift is zero, so the decoder's reference never moves. This is hue error against a still reference, not a tint you could dial back out.

fmOverdev  (FM over-deviation)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A VHS deck records brightness as FM with the video pre-emphasized, and a white-clip circuit is supposed to stop hard bright edges from overshooting the deviation the head and tape can carry. Set too hot, the overshoot runs past the response cliff and the discriminator folds back: more frequency comes out as less video. Every sharp dark-to-bright edge trails a black streak that smears rightward for about a microsecond and boils frame to frame, because the fold sits on a threshold the demod's own noise keeps re-deciding. Colour is recorded separately (colour-under), so it passes straight through the fold and the streaks carry saturated colour over black. Only sharp edges trigger it, so it lives where the picture has detail and moves with the image.

fmStreakUs  (inversion streak)
  0.1..0.7 step 0.01 us  default 0.4
  How long the demodulator takes to recover from a fold: the deemphasis time constant, which is what smears the inversion rightward. Short is a hairline shadow on every hard edge. Long drags each fold out into a black streak about a microsecond long.

## Noise & interference

noiseIre  (noise)
  0..150 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  Additive noise on the waveform, in IRE: tape grain and RF snow. Because it lands on the whole signal, enough of it will also disturb sync and confuse the colour burst. Noise degrades everything downstream.

noiseTilt  (noise spectrum (RF ↔ FM))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Where that noise floor comes from, which decides its colour. At 0 it is the RF path: noise through the tuner's IF filter, flat across the video band and grainless above it. At 1 it is the deck's own FM demodulator. Recovering frequency from phase differentiates whatever noise rides along, so the floor comes back with its energy rising toward the top of the band, the triangular spectrum every deemphasis network exists to tilt back. What survives that tilt is why tape hiss is not grey: it lives up near 3.58 MHz, lands inside the chroma bandpass, and decodes as crawling coloured speckle rather than grain. Turn it up with the comb set to notch and the floor produces colour from nothing. The level stays put as you turn it, so only the character changes.

impulseRate  (impulse noise (arcs))
  0..24 step 0.1 /frame  default 0
  Impulse interference: ignition, an arcing thermostat, a dying flyback next door. Each event is a run of signal time at carrier-scale amplitude, and its duration decides its shape on screen. Tens of microseconds is a ringing streak whose tone the decoder turns into a colour streak. Hundreds is a stepped diagonal streak folded across a few lines. Milliseconds is a torn slab of hash. The long ones land on sync tips and the beam-load measurement, so the raster tears and the sag and beam-limiter servos react to every hit. The rig reacting is most of the look. It arrives in bursts, with real quiet between.

impulseHz  (ignition train)
  0..2000 step 5 Hz  default 0
  A periodic impulse source, such as spark plugs or a commutator motor, firing at this rate. Periodic hits against the 15.734 kHz line rate land each event a fixed step sideways from the last, so the dashes line up in drifting diagonal lattices, the signature of ignition interference. The source's rate wanders like an engine revving, which tilts and shears the lattice live. Independent of the random rate above, since these are different neighbours' appliances.

strikeRate  (big strikes)
  0..20 step 0.05 /s  default 0
  Millisecond-scale events: lightning, an arcing breaker, a compressor starting. Dozens of full lines of dense hash with a DC lift, decaying down the raster. Because a strike spans whole lines it lands on sync tips and the beam-load measurement too. The PLL tears at the strike, HV sag lurches the geometry, and the beam limiter dims and blooms back. One event, and the whole rig reacts.

impulseIre  (impulse strength)
  20..400 step 1 IRE  default 90
  Peak amplitude of each impulse. Real impulses saturate the front end, so the useful range is large. Past 100 IRE every hit blooms and drags the AGC.

impulseMains  (dimmer lock)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A triac dimmer fires twice per mains cycle at its set angle, so its hits bunch at two phases of the mains instead of falling anywhere. The random hits concentrate into two bands of hash that roll through the picture with the hum bar. They share the same mains, so they move together.

## Ghosting & leakage

ghostDelayUs  (ghost delay)
  0..50 step 0.05 us  default 0
  Multipath: a reflected copy of the broadcast arriving this many microseconds late. It shows as a displaced echo to the right of everything. The further away the reflecting building, the further out the ghost.

ghostGain  (ghost gain)
  -2..2 step 0.01  default 0
  Strength of that reflection. Negative means it arrives phase-inverted, so the echo is a dark outline instead of a bright one.

humAmp  (hum)
  0..120 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  Mains hum riding on the video from a ground loop: 60 Hz on the signal, in IRE. Because it is not quite locked to the field rate it appears as a soft bright bar drifting slowly up the picture.

humMod  (hum modulation)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The same mains ripple, but in the supply of an amplifier the signal passes through, such as a failing line amp, so it moves that stage's gain instead of adding to its output. The picture pumps and its colour saturates and fades in bands rather than just brightening. Sync is scaled along with everything else, so its depth varies and the receiver's AGC and horizontal hold end up chasing the hum. Mostly 120 Hz, from the rectified supply.

soundIre  (sound carrier)
  0..40 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  The 4.5 MHz intercarrier sound leaking past the trap that is supposed to remove it. It lays a fine herringbone of interference over the picture: sound buzz you can see.

buzzLevel  (sound buzz)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The same leak heard instead of seen. This one comes out of your speakers. The sound detector recovers the 4.5 MHz beat between the picture and sound carriers, and a limiter that cannot keep the picture off it passes the video through as audio: the vertical interval as a 60 Hz buzz, line structure as a whine, and the faults above along with it. Bright scenes buzz louder because peak white really does overmodulate. Snow hisses and a head switch clicks. Fine tuning adds to it the same way it adds to the weave. The detector taps the signal rather than the tube, so a rolling picture leaves the buzz where it is. The roll happens after the sound has already been taken off.

## Dropouts & dubs

dropoutRate  (dropouts)
  0..400 step 1 /frame  default 0
  How many dropout events happen per frame. Shed oxide or a clogged head means the head reads nothing for a moment, leaving white streaks and, on a bad one, a damaged line the decoder cannot reconstruct.

dropoutComp  (dropout compensator)
  0=none 1=1-line 2=2-line  default 0
  The circuit that patches a dropout instead of letting the head's silence reach the screen. It fills the gap from a delay line holding what played a line or two ago. A line of NTSC is 227.5 subcarrier cycles, so one line back the colour arrives exactly out of phase. The patch is invisible in brightness and comes out in the complementary hue, which is the coloured streak a cheap deck leaves down a worn tape. Two lines back is a whole number of cycles, so the hue is right, at the price of a patch two lines stale, which smears across anything moving. Neither can help where the line it is holding lost the same samples, and there the raw dropout shows through.

dropoutLenUs  (dropout len)
  1..60 step 0.5 us  default 5
  How long each dropout lasts, in microseconds. A line is 63.5 µs, so 25 µs is a streak across a third of the picture width.

dubGens  (dub generations)
  1..4 step 1 x  default 1
  Runs the whole tape/channel stage this many times over: a copy of a copy of a copy. Each generation adds its own independent noise, dropouts and timebase wander on top of the last, which is why third-generation dubs fall apart much faster than one pass at triple the damage.

## RF / Tuner

rfAdjacent  (adjacent channel)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How much of the next channel up the cable gets through the IF trap. What leaks is the neighbour's carriers, and the detector turns them into beats. Their sound carrier lays a 1.5 MHz weave over everything. Their vision carrier's beat is amplitude-modulated by their raster: their blanking is peak power, so it crosses the screen as slanted dark bars, and their vertical interval as the broad sweeping band (the windshield wiper). Their line rate is not ours and wanders, so the bars slant, sweep, hang and reverse. Where their content beats into our chroma band the decoder makes colour out of it, from carrier arithmetic alone.

rfMistuneMHz  (fine tuning)
  -1..4 step 0.01 MHz  default 0
  The fine-tuning knob pulled off channel. Positive moves the 4.5 MHz sound carrier out of its trap. The buzz weave arrives on its own, and the detector starts multiplying the loose carrier against the video: chroma comes back at 920 kHz as a coarse beat, and 920 kHz picture detail comes back at 3.58 MHz, which the decoder reads as rainbow crawl on fine detail. Negative slides the picture carrier down the IF's Nyquist slope, so the upper sideband goes first. Detail softens, saturation dies, and far enough down the burst starves until the colour killer drops colour entirely.

rfSnow  (weak signal (snow))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  IF noise into the envelope detector, which is what weak-signal snow actually is. The picture rides a negative-modulation carrier, with sync at peak power and white at 12.5%, so the noise is not spread evenly. Whites boil first, blacks stay quiet longest, and sync is the last thing to go, so the picture fights through the snow instead of sinking into flat grey fuzz. Turn it up and the sync tips themselves become unreliable. The line hunt starts missing, the AGC chases a depth that no longer means anything, and the set loses the station the way a set actually loses a station.

ingress  (CB ingress)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A two-way radio getting into the cable through a cracked shield or corroded fitting. The carrier is unrelated to any NTSC frequency, so its beat draws a herringbone at no fixed angle, wandering as the transmitter drifts. It arrives in transmissions: the operator keys the mic for stretches with silence between. The program audio stands in for the speech, AM and FM at once, so the weave swells and sways when someone talks and drops back to a bare idling carrier between words.

## Cable / Wiring

polarityFlip  (hard polarity (flips sync))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  A signal/ground swap at the connector: the whole composite waveform is negated, sync pulses included. Unlike the picture-only invert above, the receiver now has to find sync in what used to be peak white, so the picture tears and rolls while it hunts.

termination  (termination (-1 daisy, +1 open))
  -1..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Composite video expects a single 75 Ω load. Negative is double-terminated, a monitor daisy-chained with its loop-through still on, which halves the signal. The picture goes dim and the colour killer starts to cut in. Positive is unterminated, so the line reflects: the signal runs hot and rings, with overshoot on every edge.

chromaPinOnly  (chroma-pin only)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  S-video miswired into a composite input, so only the chroma pin arrives. There is no luma and no sync, so the receiver free-runs on a bare subcarrier: floating colour over a black raster with nothing to lock to.

connectorGlitch  (loose connector)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How loose the plug is. Bands of lines lose contact, re-rolled every frame, the way a plug hanging on its own cable weight makes and breaks. Which of the two contacts is failing is the row below, and they fail into completely different pictures.

connectorMode  (bad contact)
  0=pin 1=shield 2=both  default 0
  Which contact of the plug is intermittent.

          - **pin**: the centre breaks the signal path, so the jack sees an
            open through its own terminator and those bands collapse to the
            input stage’s noise floor. Sync included, which is why they tear.
          - **shield**: the shell breaks the ground reference instead and
            leaves the signal alone. The return current runs to the mains earth
            through both boxes’ supplies, so a ground loop’s hum lands on the
            bad bands and the level walks and buzzes while the picture and its
            sync survive.
          - **both**: a wiggled plug, with the two faults on independent bands
            so they interleave.

scramble  (sync suppression)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How hard the head-end suppresses sync on a premium channel. The scrambler lifts the carrier during each sync pulse, so a set without a decoder box has a shallow tip, or none at all, to find the start of a line in. Under about half depth the tip still clears the slicer and the set merely mismeasures it, so the AGC over-compensates and the picture washes out bright. Past that the tip is gone and the line oscillator free-runs, so what the picture does next depends on the h-osc detune below. A set sitting exactly on 15.734 kHz coasts through the gap almost cleanly. Vertical stays roughly framed either way, because the broad vertical pulses are wider than the line-rate gate, so the frame shears instead of tumbling.

scrambleMode  (system)
  0=gated 1=alternate 2=ssavi  default 0
  Which scrambling system. Gated suppresses every line, so the oscillator free-runs the whole way down and the raster shears continuously. Alternate suppresses every other line, so the flywheel is pulled back half the time and the drift between corrections shows as a ragged line-pair zigzag on every vertical edge. It tolerates far more h-osc detune before it stops being a picture. SSAVI is Zenith's: suppression plus inversion of the active video, so what leaks through is a negative. Burst sits in the back porch and is untouched, so hue survives the inversion.

macrovision  (agc pulses (macrovision))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Macrovision's AGC poisoning, stamped on vertical-interval lines 12-19 of the source, exactly the window this receiver averages its sync depth over. A pulse parked on the back porch makes the measured sync depth balloon, so with the agc control up the set responds by crushing gain on a signal that was never hot. The pulse level walks a slow staircase, so the picture breathes instead of settling. The pulse trains sit in the blanking interval, invisible until the picture rolls and the classic flashing bar rides the vertical interval into view.

mvStripeDeg  (colorstripe)
  0..180 step 1 deg  default 0
  The later half of the process: colourbursts on moving bands of picture lines are rotated off the house phase by this much. The decoder corrects each line's hue by the burst it just gated, so the poisoned bands come out rotated the other way, as hue banding crawling down the frame. A set that trusts its burst less (burst lock) or averages bursts over lines (chroma AGC lag) is barely affected, which is the difference between the TV this was invisible on and the VCR it was aimed at.

## VHS colour & tracking

colorUnderMix  (color-under)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  VHS cannot record 3.58 MHz colour, so it heterodynes chroma down to 629 kHz, records it under the luma, and converts it back on playback. Raising this routes colour through that path. It collapses colour bandwidth to a fraction of luma's, which is why VHS colour smears sideways for many pixels while edges stay sharp.

chromaNoiseIre  (chroma noise)
  0..120 step 0.1 IRE  default 0
  Noise on the colour-under carrier itself, before it is converted back up. The 629 kHz chroma carrier gets a fraction of the headroom the luma FM does, so its signal-to-noise is far worse, which is why VHS colour is blotchy while its luma is merely grainy. This noise has to come back through the narrow chroma bandpass, so it arrives as slow smears of wrong hue rather than the fine speckle the noise slider gives. Needs colour-under raised to do anything.

underJitterDeg  (phase jitter)
  0..180 step 0.1 deg/line  default 0
  Per-line phase error in that down/up conversion. The colour-under path has to reinsert phase exactly, and when it does not, hue wanders line to line and the picture picks up a coloured venetian-blind texture. Needs colour-under raised to do anything.

ycDelayNs  (Y/C delay)
  -3360..3360 step 70 ns  default 0
  The chroma path through a deck or proc amp runs its own filters and delay lines. When their group delay is mistrimmed against the luma path the colour arrives late (or early), so every coloured area sits sideways off the edge it belongs to, bleeding out of one side of objects and falling short of the other. The burst travels the same mistrimmed path, so the decoder's reference moves with the picture's chroma and hue stays correct. Displaced colour rather than rotated, which is what tells this from a timebase error. Steps are whole samples, about 70 ns each.

trackAmt  (tracking error)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The head is not following the recorded track. It reads partly off-track, so a band of noise appears where the signal is weakest and the picture tears and bends through it. This is what the tracking knob on a VCR was for.

trackPos  (band position)
  0..1 step 0.005  default 0.85
  Where that mistracked band sits vertically, 0 top to 1 bottom. With the servo parked you park it. With the servo hunting it is where the servo is trying to sit.

trackHunt  (servo hunt)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  The deck's auto-tracking servo, searching for the track instead of holding it. It reads the RF envelope and steps until the envelope peaks. A stretched tape drifts it back off, and it corrects with less damping the higher this goes, so every correction overshoots and rings. A scene change, coming out of shuttle, the loop's splice passing, a transition cut or a thump through the cabinet from the music all knock it off the peak. The band sweeps, the picture bends through it, and the top of the frame flags on the tape tension. Draws the band by itself. Tracking error above adds a floor to it.

trackKick  (servo kick)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.6
  How hard each of those events unseats the servo. Needs servo hunt above 0.

headClog  (head clog)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  Oxide packed into the gap of one of the two spinning heads, so that head reads weak or nothing. The heads take turns, one sweep each, which is why a clogged head never shows as a steady veil. Picture and snow alternate at field rate, a hard 30 Hz flicker between the good head's sweep and the dead one's. The head switch near the bottom of the picture is where the other head is already reading, so a few last lines always belong to the opposite head: they survive the snowed sweeps and die on the clean ones. Sync goes down with the sweep, so the receiver tears through the snow instead of framing it.

shuttleX  (shuttle (1 = play))
  -32..32 step 0.05 x  default 1
  Tape speed as a multiple of play: cue past 1, pause at 0, review negative. Off play speed the spinning head no longer follows a single recorded track. Each sweep crosses several, the RF nulls at every crossing, and that many noise bars sweep the frame. Each strip between bars is a different track with its own timing and colour-under phase, so the picture tears and rainbows at the boundaries. At 1 the head tracks and the picture is clean.

## Timebase

tbJitterNs  (flutter)
  0..4000 step 5 ns  default 0
  Fast timebase error from capstan flutter, in nanoseconds. Each line starts a slightly different moment late, so edges get a ragged, shimmering wobble. This is signal-domain error: the burst moves with the picture, so hue wobbles too.

tbWowNs  (wow)
  0..10000 step 10 ns  default 0
  Slow timebase error from tape or capstan wow. Where flutter shakes line to line, wow drifts over many lines, so whole regions of the picture lean and breathe sideways together.

tbStickNs  (sticky shed)
  0..15000 step 10 ns  default 0
  Binder hydrolysis making the tape grab the head drum. Tension builds until the patch breaks free, snaps forward, and re-sticks: a relaxation oscillator, chaotic rather than periodic, and the mechanism behind squealing tapes. Down the raster that is bands of shear that lean further line by line, snap back in a few, and hang where a strong patch holds on. Signal-domain, so the colour-under phase rainbows at every slip boundary.

headSwitchShiftUs  (head switch)
  -30..30 step 0.05 us  default 0
  A helical-scan VCR swaps between two heads a few lines before the bottom of the picture, and the two do not agree on timing. That mismatch, in microseconds, is the torn hook at the very bottom of the frame that every VHS tape has.

headSwitchNoise  (switch noise)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
  How much noise hash fills the few lines during the head switch, before the servo settles on the new head. Usually hidden under the bottom of the overscan. Raise it and the frayed band shows.

## Enhancer (bent)

enhClampUs  (clamp gate)
  -60..600 step 0.1 us  default 0
  How far the box's DC-restoration gate has slid off the back porch, in microseconds. A clamp pins one sample per line to blanking and the rest of the line rides on that. Correctly set, it lands on the porch and does nothing. Drag it into active video and black level is set by whatever the picture happens to be at that instant, so the level bounces line to line with the image. Negative puts the gate on the burst or the sync tip, and the whole line lifts by the depth of sync.

enhDroopUs  (clamp droop)
  0..2000 step 1 us  default 0
  Time constant of the coupling capacitor between the gates, in microseconds. Short enough and the level sags back toward blanking within the line: bright content drags a dark streak behind it all the way to the right edge, and a lit area leaves the rest of its line depressed. This is the low-frequency smear of a box with an undersized cap. Vertical edges stay sharp.

enhPeakMHz  (detail freq (0 off))
  0..5 step 0.05 MHz  default 0
  Centre of the peaking stage the detail knob drives, with the bend's own feedback wrapped around it. A composite box has no Y/C split, so this is one knob doing two jobs. Down around 1-2 MHz it rings on picture detail and lays bars behind every edge. Up at 3.58 it boosts the subcarrier itself, so saturation climbs with detail and dot crawl comes apart.

enhPeakQ  (detail regen (0.75+ howls))
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0.5
  How much of the peaking stage's output the bend feeds back into it. Low rings for a few samples: ordinary edge overshoot. Approaching 0.75 the ring lasts most of a line. Past it the stage is regenerative. Excited by the sync pulse at the head of every line it climbs until it hits the amplifier's rails, so the bars build left to right across the picture and the image only disturbs them.

enhPeakBoost  (detail boost)
  0..16 step 0.02 x  default 0
  How much of the peaking stage is mixed back into the video. With the regen low this is a sharpness control. With it past unity this is how loud the howl is, and past about 1 the bars are full-scale and swamp the picture they came from.

enhSync  (sync regen)
  0..1 step 0.01  default 0
